22.title: Why he told stories
22.hook: Jesus rarely explained himself; he told a short story and let it sit with people (Mark 4:33–34)
22.carry: a story carries what a lecture can't
22.howItsDone: Christians read and hear the parables in church, where a Gospel passage is often read aloud and preachers return to them. Some also read one slowly at home and think about it through the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mark 1:1: the beginning of the good news, the first line of the shortest Gospel. Your line was start here. That closed Camp 1 at twenty-one words.

A lake in Galilee, early in the day. The crowd is so big the teacher can't stand on the beach anymore. So he climbs into a fishing boat, pushes off, and sits in it, while the whole crowd stands at the water's edge. Farmers. Fishermen. Mothers with children on their hips. People who came because a neighbor said you have to hear this man. What does he give them? Not a lecture. Not a list of rules. He says: listen. A farmer went out to sow. A story that takes about a minute. Then he stops, and doesn't explain it. That's how the Gospels say he taught, over and over. Camp 2 is those stories. Today, why he told them.
screen: `A BOAT. A CROWD ON THE SHORE.` → `NOT A LECTURE.` → `A FARMER WENT OUT TO SOW.`

segments.voice: Parable comes from the Greek parabole: something thrown alongside. You throw a small, ordinary picture alongside something too big to look at straight. A seed. A lost coin. A party. Behind it sits a Hebrew word teachers already used, mashal, which covers proverbs, riddles and short stories. His listeners knew the form. In the King James: "And with many such parables spake he the word unto them, as they were able to hear it. But without a parable spake he not unto them." As they were able to hear it. That's the first thing a parable does: it meets people where they are. A farmer knows seed. A woman who has swept a floor knows what it is to lose a coin. Nobody needs a degree to walk in. Second, it stays. A rule is forgotten by lunch. A shepherd walking into the dark after one sheep follows you home, and you're still turning it over on Tuesday. Third, the twist. Somebody gets paid too much. The wrong man turns out to be the good one. You have to decide what you think, and sometimes the story turns round and asks where you're standing. Mark adds one more thing: alone with his closest followers, he explained it all. The crowd got the story; the students got the story and the questions. Christians often read the parables as something to live with, not just solve. Some take under a minute to read. The next two weeks are those stories, one a day.

Your line: a story carries what a lecture can't. See you tomorrow for the first one: the sower.

23.title: The sower (Matthew 13:1–9)
23.hook: seed lands on path, rock, thorns and good soil; most is wasted, and the harvest is huge anyway
23.tomorrow: The mustard seed and the yeast (Matthew 13:31–33)
23.howItsDone: The parable of the sower is told in Matthew, Mark and Luke and read aloud in churches; Christians hear it as a question about how they receive the word, and as encouragement to keep sharing it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, parable: a small story thrown alongside something too big to look at straight. Today, the first of them.

A farmer walks the edge of his field, a bag of seed on his hip. He takes a handful and flings it in a wide arc. He isn't placing seeds. He's throwing. Some lands on the hard footpath, and the birds have it before he finishes the row. Some lands where rock sits under a skin of soil: it shoots up fast, and the first hot day kills it. Some lands among thorns and gets strangled. And some lands in good ground. Plenty of the listeners had done this with their own hands. They knew how much seed a farmer loses. They didn't expect the ending.
screen: `A FARMER THROWING SEED.` → `PATH, ROCK, THORNS, GOOD GROUND.` → `THEY DIDN'T EXPECT THE ENDING.`

segments.voice: It opens, in the King James: "Behold, a sower went forth to sow." Three kinds of ground out of four fail. Keep count and it's a story about waste. Then the last line: the good ground "brought forth fruit, some an hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold." Some readers hear a hundredfold as the kind of number that makes a farmer laugh out loud. Everyone knew about failure. The surprise is a harvest that dwarfs it. Later in the same chapter, the Gospel gives an explanation, told to the disciples. The seed is the word, the good news of God's kingdom. The grounds are kinds of listeners: one hears and loses it at once, one is thrilled for a week, one lets worries choke it, one lets it grow. Christians hear the story from two sides, sometimes both at once. About the sower: keep throwing, even when most of it seems wasted, because you can't see where the good ground is. About the soil: what kind of ground am I, today? And notice: the farmer doesn't test the soil or save his seed for the good patch. He throws it on path, rock and thorns, as if there's plenty to go around. It ends: "Who hath ears to hear, let him hear." The story stops, and hands the question to you.

segments.voice: Let your breathing slow, and picture the four grounds: the hard path, too trampled to take anything in; thin soil over rock; the thorns, plenty of life but the worries winning; the good earth, open and ready. Without grading yourself, notice which one you are today. It's only today: ground changes, paths get broken up, thorns get pulled, so let yourself be whatever ground you are.
The sower. A farmer throwing seed everywhere, as if there's plenty, and a harvest that dwarfs the waste.
Your line: keep throwing seed. That's the first story of Camp 2, and day twenty-three, done.

24.title: The mustard seed and the yeast (Matthew 13:31–33)
24.hook: the smallest seed becomes a bush for birds; a pinch of yeast lifts a mountain of dough
24.howItsDone: Christians hear these two short parables read together in church, and many see in them a picture of how faith and the church grow: quietly, from small beginnings. Some keep a mustard seed as a reminder.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sower: seed thrown on every kind of ground, most of it lost, and a harvest anyway. Your line was keep throwing seed.

A man plants a mustard seed, a speck you could lose under a fingernail. It grows until it's bigger than everything else in the garden, like a small tree, and birds settle in its branches. A woman making bread works a little lump of yeast into a huge heap of flour, covers it, and leaves it. Slowly, while nobody's watching, the whole heap rises. Two stories, each about as long as a breath. And Jesus says: this is what the kingdom of heaven is like.
screen: `A SPECK OF A SEED.` → `BIRDS IN THE BRANCHES.` → `A LUMP OF YEAST. A HEAP OF FLOUR.`

segments.voice: Leaven is the old word for yeast, or for a lump of sour dough kept back from yesterday's batch to start today's. The King James: "The kingdom of heaven is like unto leaven, which a woman took, and hid in three measures of meal, till the whole was leavened." Three things hide in that sentence. First, hid. Not mixed. You can't see leaven work; for hours nothing seems to happen. Second, three measures. In Genesis, that's what Abraham asks Sarah to bake when three strangers turn up at his tent: bread for honored guests. A feast, from one small lump. Third, a surprise. At Passover, Jewish families clear leaven out of the house, remembering bread baked in haste on the way out of Egypt. And elsewhere Jesus uses leaven as a warning, something spreading where you don't want it. Here he turns it around: the quiet thing that spreads through everything is the kingdom. The mustard seed does the same trick in the open. The text calls it "the least of all seeds," and says it becomes a tree where "the birds of the air come and lodge." Gardeners know smaller seeds; the story talks the way a farmer does, about the speck in his palm. So the point comes twice: in a field and in a kitchen, by a man and by a woman. What God is doing, Christians say, starts small enough to miss, grows quietly, and ends up big enough to shelter others.

Leaven. A little lump of yeast, hidden in the dough, that lifts the whole batch.
Your line: small is how it starts. Two small stories, one big idea; that's day twenty-four.

25.title: The lost sheep (Luke 15:3–7)
25.hook: a shepherd leaves ninety-nine in the open to go after one
25.howItsDone: Christians often picture Jesus as the Good Shepherd, and this parable is read in churches as a picture of God searching for anyone who has wandered off. Many churches take its name for their outreach to people who have stopped coming.

segments.voice: Yesterday, leaven: a little lump hidden in the flour that lifts the whole batch. Small is how it starts.

Ten friends in a group chat, jokes every night. Then one stops replying. No fight. They just drift, and after a week the chat rolls on without them. Most of us have been on both sides of that. Now a shepherd at dusk, counting his flock in: ninety-seven, ninety-eight, ninety-nine. One short. It's getting dark, and any sensible person would call it a good day and shut the gate. He doesn't. He leaves the ninety-nine in the open country and walks back out into the hills, after one.
screen: `THE FRIEND WHO STOPPED REPLYING.` → `NINETY-NINE. ONE SHORT.` → `HE WALKS BACK OUT.`

segments.voice: Luke says why Jesus told it. People with bad reputations, tax collectors and others everyone called sinners, kept coming close to listen, and some of the religious teachers grumbled: "This man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them." Remember day ten: he ate with the wrong people on purpose. This story is his answer, and it opens with a question: "What man of you, having an hundred sheep, if he lose one of them, doth not leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness, and go after that which is lost, until he find it?" Until he find it. Not until it's too dark. And wilderness here means open grazing land, not a jungle. The risk is real: the ninety-nine are left on their own. Then the part people forget. He doesn't scold the sheep or drag it home. "He layeth it on his shoulders, rejoicing." A grown sheep is heavy; he carries it anyway, happy. At home he calls his friends and neighbors: "Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost." Jesus ends plainly: more joy in heaven over one person who turns back than over ninety-nine who never needed to. His listeners knew the old picture, the Psalm that begins "The Lord is my shepherd," and Christians have seen God in this shepherd ever since. Some of the oldest Christian paintings, in the Roman catacombs, show a young shepherd with a sheep across his shoulders. As math, one in a hundred is terrible. But the story isn't doing math. To God, nobody is a rounding error.
screen: `THIS MAN EATS WITH SINNERS.` · `UNTIL HE FIND IT.` · `ON HIS SHOULDERS, REJOICING.` · then, large: `NOBODY IS A ROUNDING ERROR.`

segments.voice: Scroll back, in your head, through the people who used to be around: a friend from school, a cousin, a coworker who moved on. Let one face come up, someone who drifted, not someone who hurt you, and hold them in mind for a few breaths. If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, wish them well, wherever they are tonight.

26.title: The lost coin (Luke 15:8–10)
26.hook: a woman lights a lamp, sweeps the whole house for one coin, then throws a party
26.howItsDone: Christians read the lost coin together with the lost sheep and the prodigal son, the three stories of Luke 15, as pictures of God searching for people and rejoicing when they come home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, wilderness: the open land where a shepherd left ninety-nine to walk back out after one. Your line was one is worth the walk.

Keys. They were on the counter a minute ago. Pockets, twice. Couch cushions. Hands and knees with a phone flashlight, peering under the fridge. Then there they are, and the whole morning changes. Right after the lost sheep, Luke tells a second story, indoors. A woman has ten silver coins, and one is gone. She lights a lamp, grabs a broom, and sweeps the whole house until she finds it. Then she does something nobody does with found keys. She throws a party.
screen: `THE KEYS WERE RIGHT HERE.` → `TEN COINS. ONE GONE.` → `SHE THROWS A PARTY.`

segments.voice: The King James: "Either what woman having ten pieces of silver, if she lose one piece, doth not light a candle, and sweep the house, and seek diligently till she find it?" A drachma is a small silver coin. Not a fortune, but not nothing to her. She has three tools: a lamp, a broom, and patience, and she keeps going until. Why does one coin matter so much? The story doesn't say. Some suggest her savings, or part of a family set, but that's a guess. Then the party: "she calleth her friends and her neighbours together, saying, Rejoice with me; for I have found the piece which I had lost." The party may well have cost more than the coin, and some readers think that's the point: the joy is bigger than the thing. Jesus ends it: "there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner that repenteth." Here's the quiet surprise. Yesterday the searcher was a shepherd. Today it's a woman sweeping her kitchen. Christians often read the shepherd as a picture of God, and some readers, ancient and modern, notice that this story, told right beside it, gives the same searching love a woman's face. Same crowd, too: people grumbling about who he ate with. His answer, twice now: when someone is found, you don't file it away. You call the neighbors.

27.title: The treasure and the pearl (Matthew 13:44–46)
27.hook: a man finds treasure in a field and, in joy, sells everything to buy it
27.howItsDone: Christians read these two parables as a picture of how much God's kingdom is worth, and some tell stories of people who left careers or comforts gladly to follow their faith. They're read in churches in the season when Matthew 13 comes around in the lectionary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a drachma: one small silver coin, a whole house swept to find it. Your line was throw the party.

A man is working a field that isn't his. Long day, hard ground. His tool hits something that isn't a rock. He digs around it with his hands: a hoard, buried who knows how long ago, by who knows whom. He looks around. Nobody saw. He covers it back up, walks home, and sells everything he owns. The house. The animals. The good coat. The neighbors think he's lost his mind. He's grinning the whole time, because he knows what's in that field, and he buys it. Right beside it, Jesus tells another: a merchant seeking fine pearls finds one of great price, and sells everything for it too.
screen: `A TOOL HITS SOMETHING.` → `HE SELLS EVERYTHING.` → `A MERCHANT FINDS ONE PEARL.`

segments.voice: Each story takes a verse or two in Matthew, and the two men arrive in opposite ways. The farmhand wasn't looking; he stumbled on it. The merchant was out seeking goodly pearls, as the King James puts it. Christians hear both: some are found by faith on an ordinary afternoon, some search for years. Then the line the story turns on. Having found the treasure, the man "for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath." For joy. Not because he was told to. Not a sacrifice he grits his teeth through. He's trading up, and he knows it. Sell everything sounds like loss; the story hears a man who can't believe his luck. So what's the treasure? Jesus says the kingdom of heaven is like this. One reading: God's kingdom, God's life, is worth more than everything you own, and finding it feels like joy. Another turns it around: God is the one who gives everything to buy back the field, or the one "pearl of great price" is each person, and the one who sells all to have it is Christ. Both readings are still preached. One more detail. Matthew's Greek word for treasure is thesauros: a store, a hoard, something laid up. Earlier in the same Gospel, Jesus says: "where your treasure is, there will your heart be also." So the two stories ask one quiet question. What would make you that happy to let go?

segments.voice: Ask yourself what you'd give everything for, and let the answer come up on its own instead of reaching for the right one: a person, a way of living, a kind of peace. If you pray, hold it before God and ask whether it's the treasure. Either way, notice how naming it feels: heavy, like duty, or light, like the man walking home from the field.

cover it up, sell everything you own, and buy the field.
tell the owner and hope for a reward.
fork.reveal: he hides it again and, "for joy thereof," sells all he has and buys the field. the story doesn't stop to judge his ethics. it's about the joy.

original.note: Greek: treasure, a store of valuables. the word in Matthew 13:44, and in 6:21: where your treasure is.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about giving everything up.
what it means: a story about joy. he sells everything because he's found something worth more.
what a scholar hears: two readings, both still preached. the buyer is a person finding the kingdom, or the buyer is God, and the pearl of great price is us.
guess: a hoard of riches stored up and kept
a debt owed to the owner of the field
a gift of money left at the temple
recall: ekklesia: the people called out, gathered
the morning the tomb was found empty

chat.says: Selling everything for one treasure sounds like a huge sacrifice. Is that the point?
options: Not really. He sells it all for joy, because he knows he's trading up.
Yes. It teaches that faith means painfully giving up what you love.
Yes. It's a warning about risking everything on one big gamble.
chat.meaning: The man sells everything "for joy thereof." Not a sacrifice he grits his teeth through: he's trading up, and he knows it.

thesauros.meaning: Matthew's Greek word for treasure: a store, a hoard laid up

pearl of great price.meaning: the one precious pearl the merchant sells everything to buy

Matthew.meaning: one of the four Gospels, where these two stories are told

28.title: Workers in the vineyard (Matthew 20:1–16)
28.hook: those hired at the last hour get a full day's pay, and the early ones grumble
28.howItsDone: Christians often read this parable as a picture of God's grace, given the same to people who come to faith late as to those who came early. It's a common text for sermons on envy, fairness and welcome.

segments.voice: Yesterday, thesauros: a field's treasure, and a man who sold everything for it. Your line was in joy, not duty.

Dawn, in a village square. Men wait, hoping for a day's work. A landowner hires a crew for his vineyard, and they agree the usual wage: one silver coin, a day's pay. At nine he's back for more. At noon, more. At three, more. At five, with one hour of light left, men are still standing there. Why are you idle all day? Because no one hired us. So he sends them in too. At sunset the pay line forms, and he tells his manager: start with the last. The five o'clock crew each get one silver coin, a full day's pay for one hour. The dawn crew start doing the math. Then they get paid. One coin each.
screen: `DAWN, NINE, NOON, THREE, FIVE.` → `START WITH THE LAST.` → `ONE COIN EACH.`

segments.voice: The complaint, in the King James, is hard to argue with: "These last have wrought but one hour, and thou hast made them equal unto us, which have borne the burden and heat of the day." They have a point. It isn't fair, and the owner doesn't pretend it is. He says: friend, I did you no wrong; you agreed to a coin. Then a sharp question: "is thine eye evil, because I am good?" Why does my generosity to them feel like a loss to you? Christians read it more than one way. Some hear grace: God's welcome isn't a wage earned by the hour, and someone who comes to faith on their last day is welcomed like someone who came as a child. Others hear who belongs: old insiders and newcomers made equal. Some notice the money: one coin was the day's wage they all agreed on, so the latecomers go home with a full day's pay, like everyone else. Churches hold these readings side by side. And the English phrase the eleventh hour, for just in time, is often traced to this crew, hired at the eleventh hour of the working day. That closes a week of stories: why he told them at all, seed on every ground, a mustard seed and a pinch of yeast, a shepherd after one sheep, a woman sweeping for one coin, a treasure worth everything, and now a boss who pays the last first. In almost every one, somebody gives more than makes sense.
screen: `THEY HAVE A POINT. IT ISN'T FAIR.` · `IS THINE EYE EVIL, BECAUSE I AM GOOD?` · `GRACE, BELONGING, A FULL DAY'S PAY.` · `A WEEK OF STORIES THAT OVERPAY.` · then, large: `THE LAST SHALL BE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Think of the ledger you carry: who does the dishes, who texted last, who got the credit, who got off easy. Find one line and, without erasing it, feel what keeping it costs you. If you pray, hand it to God; if not, loosen your grip, a little.
Denarius. The silver coin, a full day's wage, that every worker goes home with, hired at dawn or at the eleventh hour.
Your line: generosity isn't fair. it's better. A week of stories, wrapped; see you on day twenty-nine.

fork.setup: you're the owner at sunset. the dawn crew are angry that the five o'clock crew got the same coin. what do you say?
options: you're right. here's a bonus.
fine. next time the late ones get less.
friend, I did you no wrong. is your eye evil because I am good?
fork.reveal: he doesn't pretend it's fair. he says they got what they agreed to, and asks why his generosity feels like their loss.

original.note: Greek, from the Latin denarius: a silver coin, a laborer's day's pay. the old King James calls it a penny.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about bad management.
what it means: generosity that ignores the ledger. the owner gives the last what they need, and the first what they agreed.
what a scholar hears: the KJV's "penny" is a denarius, the day's wage they agreed on (Matthew 20:2). the last are paid first, and paid the same.
guess: a silver coin, a laborer's pay for one day
a gold coin worth a whole season of work
a tax paid to Rome after each harvest
recall: euangelion: good news, announced to all
ekklesia: the people called out, gathered

chat.says: Why did the vineyard owner pay the one-hour workers the same as everyone?
options: He chose to be generous, and no one got less than they agreed to.
He lost track of who started when, and paid everyone by mistake.
The late workers worked twice as hard to make up the time.
chat.meaning: The dawn crew got the coin they agreed to. The owner asks, "is thine eye evil, because I am good?" It's generosity, not a wage.

denarius.meaning: a silver coin, a full day's wage

vineyard.meaning: a farm where grapevines are grown

eleventh hour.meaning: the last hour of the working day; now, just in time

grace.meaning: a gift you didn't earn, freely given
